Hannibal. Hannibal Barca lived from around two hundred forty-seven to one hundred eighty-three BCE. A Carthaginian general and strategist, his invasion of Italy during the Second Punic War brought Rome to the brink of destruction. His tactical genius, especially the double envelopment at Cannae, made him one of history's greatest military commanders, though political constraints and lack of reinforcements ultimately prevented him from conquering Rome itself.

Born into the Barcid family, his father Hamilcar Barca was Carthage's leading general. Hannibal swore an oath to oppose Rome and spent his youth in Spain as his father expanded Carthaginian holdings. He inherited command at roughly age twenty-five in two hundred eighteen BCE.

That year, he invaded Italy with roughly forty thousand troops and war elephants after marching across Spain and the Alps. His dramatic crossing cost significant losses but achieved strategic surprise by bringing the war directly to Roman territory. At the Battle of Cannae in August two hundred sixteen BCE, Hannibal's tactical masterpiece saw him draw Roman forces into a center and then envelop them with cavalry attacks on both flanks, annihilating roughly fifty thousand Roman soldiers. It was Rome's worst defeat in the war.

Despite this victory, Hannibal could not take Rome itself. Italian allied cities defected to him, but Rome's resilience, local fortifications, and his lack of siege equipment constrained his options. He became bogged down in a war of attrition he could not win.

Roman Scipio Africanus eventually invaded North Africa to threaten Carthage itself, forcing Hannibal to return home. Scipio defeated him at Zama in two hundred two BCE, ending the Second Punic War and Carthage's status as a great power.

After the war, Hannibal served as a magistrate in Carthage, then fled to the Seleucid court as Rome's enemy and eventually to Bithynia, where he died in exile, reportedly by suicide rather than capture.
